Grup de fete din Ofcea îmbrăcate cu cămăși cu mâneci treisferturi, poale albe, șort în dungi sau cu buline, veste simple sau cu motive florale, iar la gât salbă cu bani. Pe fundal apar câțiva bărbați care au cămașă albă, vestă neagră și pălărie. Pe paspartu, sub fotografie însemnări manuscrise cu tuș negru privind localitatea, datarea, fotograful. Fotografia prezintă urme de degradare. Pe verso ștampilă incomplet vizibilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.355" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată); însemnări manuscrise. cu creionul: "271 ASTRA / Exp. Astra 1905 cat. I B 57". Număr inventar MCPR 554.

R: Grup de fete tinere "de măritiș", îmbrăcate în port popular de sărbătoare din Banatul sârbesc. Fotografie de exterior, realizată într-un cadru natural. Fotografia este prinsă de un carton de culoare crem. Cartonul are patru tăieturi pentru a fixa coțurile fotografiei. V: Pe verso însemnări manuscrise în creion ("Banat / Glogon / No. 1 / 274 ASTRA), însemnare manuscrisă cu stiloul "Fete și feciori din Ofcea - Comint. Timiș-Torantal / Cercul Panciova / Foto ing. Th. Gabarekwe Kgaga, a San woman living in Matlapaneng, with her child, standing outside her lolwapa (small front courtyard) made from tshikitshane (Stipagrostis uniplumis) grass bundles recovered from a dilapidated neighbour's roof. She built this house using drinks cans for walling from a local bar, due to the difficulty of finding letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) at the river.

View (looking northward) of buildings around the main plaza of San Felipe pueblo, with the Rio Grande river in the distance, and Santa Ana Mesa visible in the distance on the left.  In the foreground a group of villagers is gathered, and closer still to the camera the collector James Stevenson can be seen talking with a local inhabitant.  According to Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'dwellings of this village never reach higher than two stor[ey]s', and the 'walls of the old pueblo are constructed of well-selected lava bo[u]lders of uniform size'.  The photograph was probably taken by John Hillers from the roof of the Catholic church.

A portrait of a carrier with baggage on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.

Three young women, one carrying a gourd vessel, another with a carrying ring on her head, wearing bead-fringed skirts. This village was the clan centre of the important Jowatcuaa clan (named after it's lineage founder, Ocala) although it had no headman but prominent clan elders.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree (with a ?Sycamore to the right), located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.

A portrait of a seated man (identified as King Aguaa-war-Akuon of Obuodhi village) sitting on a stool with another royal stool beside him and a leopard skin laid out in front. Mbila. A xylophone with ten wooden keys, suspended and attached to a frame with fibre lacing. The keys are all the same length, but get gradually thicker, the thickest keys making the lowest-pitched notes. The keys are suspended over a central, longitudinal strut with bored holes for each key that connect to the respective, graded-size gourd resonators underneath. Each gourd has a small hole with a black membrane stretched over; however, only one membrane is intact. Each gourd has an additional gourd ring adhered to it with black wax or resin, to act as a case to protect the membrane, but only one of these now remains. Additional strips of wood with shallow notches along the upper edge are also leather-laced and attached to the strut, arranging the keys in pairs. The strut ends connect with an U-shaped wooden frame (handle) with shallow notches along the upper edges of sides.

Slit drum carved from a single piece of wood, used for signalling. The drum section is a hollow half-cylinder with a long oblong slit across the top. The drum is two-toned, with the side on one half of the slit being about one tone higher than the other. It is supported on two legs, and has a handle in the form of a carved human head at each end. There is a vertical perforation through the neck of each handle; however, one of them is blocked. There are incised numerals on each side.
Ndu kuna. Gourd container with circular opening where the stem originally was. Lengths of bark fibre tied around waist. Ndu kuna.
Ngu. A piece of curved wood with a length of raffia tied around it. Used in a game; the user throws it to the ground, and tries to catch it in a noose when it bounces back upward.
Wilingwa ka kpe akoro. Wooden pot scraper with handle and flat paddle with square end. Used to scrape outside of pots. Accretions.
Grass circumcision skirt. Alternating groups of light and dark lengths of grass tied to a cord waistband. Used by boys for dancing. Tied in a roll.

A full length portrait of a Zande woman in the entrance to a homestead, wearing coiled metal arm and ankle rings and leaf pubic covering on a string. Set to both sides of the entrance are two shields leaning against the fence, which is made from stalks etc. The shield to the left seems to have a throwing knife placed on top of it. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A man (possibly Kisanga) immersing a basket of malted eleusine grain which is wrapped in banana leaves, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew. It is then spread out in the sun to germinate.
A woman wearing a striped woven cloth (ramu) and a small boy carrying a stick, with other dancers in the background, with one possibly seated on a wooden gong (gugu).
Portrait of a boy (identified as wiri Zaba, i.e. a son of Zaba) wearing a white cotton waist cloth.
The back of a man's head (identified as Kamanga's), with his hand shading his eyes.
A portrait of a youth (identified as Khamsa) in shirt and shorts standing in front of a reed courtyard fence.

A tuka or spirit shrine, consisting of a forked tree trunk or branch, with a bowl containing offerings set in the fork. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. This shrine has numerous medicines growing around it, including sarawa, ranga ambiri and giango (cactus plant).

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.

A Zande version of the widespread African game often known as mancala (an arabic word meaning 'to transfer', i.e. move game pieces from one hole to another). The Zande version (known as abanga) was sometimes carved, but is here set in the earth under the eaves of a hut or granary, with an old-style stool for a player visible beyond.

Figure carved from wood. Seated figure holding a mask with beard over their face; mask has scarification marks on both cheeks; beard decorated with hatched pattern. Narrow slots burnt into either side of head, possibly for missing attachment.

Two whistles, made from scraped and cleaned kaffir oranges. Both are spherical in shape and have one large central hole and one smaller side hole. Used on night marshes to the coast to frighten wild beasts away from the path, the first and last person for the group of travellers being provided with an instrument.

A beer palm wine strainer, consisting of a long basketry funnel made from plant fibre. The wider, open end is rolled over and has a plant fibre fringe. There is a plaited plant fibre loop attached the narrower, closed end.

A comb carved from wood. It has five pointed prongs, and a square handle with two inward-pointing triangular projections at the top. The handle is decorated with an incised geometric design on both sides.
Portrait of a woman wearing tukakao or chikobwela (wound copper or iron wire earrings) and a kakuze (a patterned bead necklace) holding a child whose hair is braided with beads or shells.

A woman wearing a number of bead necklaces, tukakao or chikobwela (wound copper or iron wire earrings), a tusambo (an armband), and a number of bracelets hugs a crying child whilst mixing nsima (porridge) or relish in a metal pot. The porridge is made from a flour (of maize, millet or sorghum) mixed with water from the nongo (water pot) next to her right foot.

An old woman watches as two boys play on ngoma (pegged, single membrane drums) in front of a ng' anda (a ground-house) with a verandah. The boy on the left plays a small badima drum (a pedestal-based drum used at formal and children's dances) and the boy on the right a masabe drum (one of a set of three drums of differing pitches often associated with the masabe cult of spirit possession).
A young woman wearing a kakata (a cowrie shell headpad), tusambo (armband), mulapi (an apron) and manda (skirt) winnows the seed from the chaff through a tray into a cisuo basket.

A young woman wearing a kakata (a cowrie shell headpad), tukakao or chikobwela (wound copper or iron wire earrings), a beaded cisita (a reed nose plug), a spiral patterned munkonde (a beaded rope necklace) and a number of kakuze (bead ropes) around her waist. Beaded cisita were usually only worn on special occasions and consisted of a normal reed nose plug covered with a sleeve of beads.

Portrait of a woman wearing tukakao or chikobwela (wound copper or iron wire earrings), a kakuze (a patterned bead necklace) and tusambo (bracelets) bearing a large nogo or inongo (water pot) on her head.

A smiling woman wearing tusambo (bracelets) bears two cisuo (baskets) on her head.

Musical bow with a brass wire string. The bow is wooden, and curves round at either end. There is a small notch in both ends to keep the string in place. The string has broken and some of it is missing. The bow should also have a gourd resonator (E 1916.31.19 B) but it is missing.

A woman sitting in front of a structure made of corrugated metal sheets, holding a blue mug of coffee on Philip's Farm, Namibia. She wears a floral blue top, patterned blue skirt, red head scarf and a white patterned apron.

An upper body profile portrait of a seated Baka girl wearing a leaf covering front and rear. In the companion full face image she seems to have been photographed against a sheet marked with metric measurements (visible to the right) for recording height. This is the only photograph in the collection which shows this anthropometric measurement, but suggests that some of the other images may have originally have been taken to also provide such 'scientific' data. Composite textile. Two strips of woven textile alternating with three bands of crochet; central band of crochet has a diamond pattern.

A guitar made from wood, leather, hair and iron. The body is formed from a hollowed piece of wood, with piece of leather stretched across the opening and held taught with little wooden pegs. The neck is formed from a straight piece of wood and sits below the leather, with a bridge of wood attached and exiting from a hole cut into the leather.  The neck has four ties of leather strips which originally held the strings of plaited hair in place. Broken sections of string remain attached and there is a small iron wire loop at the side of the body.

Small, decorated wooden door. The door is made from a rectangular piece of wood with wooden strips (two with serrated edges) attached with metal staples near the edges to form a frame.  The surface is carved with geometric designs and painted with black and red pigments.

Portrait of a smiling Mandara woman. She has a small tuft of hair on their head, facial scarifications and tattoos, and nose and upper and lower lip piercings with circular white plugs, and is wearing a red and yellow beaded necklace.

View of ruined and partially built huts using drinks cans as main walling material, in the plot belonging to Tumelo Samoxhose (born 1968), a Yeyi man living in Wenela Ward (visible in background). Tumelo's father was from Malawi and mother from Seronga. He migrated to Matlapaneng Ward in Maun in 1982, coming to Wenela in 1992.

Two grandsons of Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) ploughing with donkeys in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. The grandson holding the plough is Boitlhoko Kgalalo, the one leading the donkeys is Lekgoana Kgalalo. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.
Portrait of two of Bailelwa Gabanakgosi's children.

A large concrete block house under construction in the plot belonging to the Garebakwena family in Wenela ward. Morton's fieldwork assistant, Boitlhoko Garebakwena, lived here and contributed some of the money he earned towards the costs of the house. Multi-room houses of this size were quite unusual in most wards of Maun at the time.
An elderly man in the household of Odirilwe Mbwe in Sanyedi ward.

A full length oblique rear view portrait of a Bari girl standing in a homestead wearing an apron of metal chain links at the front, with a 'tail' of strings behind. She is also wearing a number of neck ornaments as well as metal wrist and ankle rings. It seems likely that this image was taken shortly before October 1878 when Buchta reached Lado (Juba) on board S.S. Safia.

A homestead grave in the village of Ali Bey, consisting of two notched stakes to which are tied a long peeled stick, and a sapling on which is hung pieces of slag. At the foot is a pot containing sacrifice, and also two groups of cooking stones, indicating two sacrifices have been made. The Seligmans carried out investigations among the Bari of Belinian and Ali Bey in Jan 1922, before moving south to the Torit area among the Lotuko-speaking people there.

An upper body full face portrait of a seated Bari woman wearing a large belt of bead strings, tied together at the front. A man, Engulé, with a tall spear standing behind an earth or termite mound. The mound may even have been shaped by elephants using their tusks. A large blade being held is also visible in the bottom right hand corner of the frame.
View across the bai (natural clearing in the forest). Dense forest vegetation is visible in the background.

A large gathering of women and children underneath a shelter made from logs with a thatched roof and open sides. Most of the group are facing forward and looking in the same direction towards someone or something out of frame to the left of the image. In the left hand side of the image a woman wearing a dress of printed material is standing up and is speaking. In the background there are buildings made from wooden logs and mud with thatched roofs. According to Louis Sarno, the women are probably acting out a story with mime. Named individuals include: Mbongi, Mafiki, Esusi, Mbina, Sepi and others. The women only gather here when there are no men present. This image is similar to image 1997.21.3.612-614 and 1997.21.3.615.

View across the clearing of settlement looking towards a large group of people sitting underneath a shelter made of wooden poles with a roof and open sides. One woman is standing on her own in the clearing to the left of the shelter and appears to be addressing a smaller group sat outside the shelter in the right of the image. A large basket and a metal vessel lies on the floor in the right of the image. This image is similar to image 1997.21.3.626.

Domestic scene outside some dome-shaped shelters at the edge of a clearing in the forest. In the bottom left of the image a woman is sat on the ground weaving a large basket. Six children are stood together in a group in the centre close to some mats or other material. The shelters are made from branches that are bent into arcs to form a framework that is covered with leaves. Just behind the shelters in the left of the image some clothing hangs on a line. Kazinaw is fourth from the left in the beam of light.
View looking up a tree trunk in the forest towards the forest canopy and the sky above.

View of forest vegetation including palm trees with narrow fronds. In the centre of the frame there is a cluster of fruits supported by the branches of a tree. This image is similar to images 1997.21.3.751-752.

This man is definitely not a Luo judging from his personal body adornment. It is probable that Evans-Pritchard met this man on the road somewhere, perhaps even in Luo country. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This group is a mixture of married Luo women, young girls and children, posed in a line standing and seated, at Karungu in south Nyanza. Here the use of  skin or fibre aprons (olemo), armlets (minyonge) and bead necklaces (tik ng’ut) is very evident, and in fact some girls and women have adopted a whole waist skin wrap. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05 & CM 27/04/2007]

A portrait of a Luo man wearing bead ornaments around the neck and waist, an upper arm leather/hide bangle, metal leg rings and armlets (minyonge) and a skin apron both at the back and front. The man is sitting on a stool in front of a colonial administrative building, almost certainly at the newly established centre in Kisumu. The building is carefully constructed from local materials, including bundles of lake reeds surrounding the roof supports to form an open verandah, and stone work beneath.  [Gilbert Oteyo 24/04/2005 CM 24/04/2007]
Looking down from a ridge across large boulders towards Lake Kanyaboli. [CM 13/03/2007]

A portrait of a man wearing Luo ornamentation, on the road next to a vehicle. On his head is worn a bead work hat (ogut tigo) with the extended skin ledge in which warthog teeth (leke njiri) are stuck protruding out and curving upwards. The ears are adorned with multicoloured beads sewn on a tiny chain usually forming a beautiful earring (ngaga) for old men. He has a walking stick on the shoulder (okwajo) on which he is hanging a woven shopping basket (okapo). He has a necklace (rek) made of ostrich egg shell, and a round block of something suspended on the necklace as well. He also has a sheathed dagger hanging a cross his shoulder. There is a metal wrist ring (minyonge) and the fingers are all heavily adorned with all sorts of metal rings (tere). His bodily clothing remains mainly European. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Looking from the top of a ridge towards Kendu Bay, a small township in South Nyanza District. It is on the shore of Lake Victoria and had a small pier and a steamship service connecting it with Kisumu. The clear plain area and lake shore area of it is seen here with the lake water in the distance. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
An upper body portrait of a young Luo man wearing a European shirt standing in front of a thatched house. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A full length portrait of a Luo man identified as Ocieng, dressed in the manner of an elder attending a funeral ceremony. His hat is probably made of fur and has two warthog teeth (leke njiri or leke mbeche) stuck on it, hanging down in front of his forehead. He is clad in a leopard skin (lpien kwach) and has a pair of skin sandals on his feet. He wears a number of metal wrist rings (minyonge) on both hands. Although he seems dressed for a funeral ceremony, the strip of animal skin worn hanging from his neck does mean some sort of animal has been slaughtered for this man in a cleansing ceremony. This means that he could be a warrior or a man possessed by spirits. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A typical Luo homestead (dala) with a thick euphorbia fence surrounding grass thatch huts, set on the upper slopes of the undulating Luo countryside. The rest of the village is seen spread over the landscape. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A vignette upper body portrait of an Acholi chief, identified as Faiso, wearing an animal skin and a cowrie decorated headdress surmounted by a feather or fibre contrasting plume. A display of a number of Acholi domestic objects set out on a table during Buchta's journey through Acholi country sometime in January 1879 en route to Bunyoro. The objects include pots (one with a double aperture), gourd vessels, a wooden bowl with stand (monoxylous), a pipe, feather headdress, fly whisk and cowrie-decorated arm band with hair attachment. They are displayed on a camp-style packable table with a large sheet backing.

Looking towards the huts of an Acholi village at the foot of a hill, called by Buchta Choua (Chua or Shua) Hill, in Chua County of northern Uganda. The huts are closely spaced, mostly step-thatched, and smaller granaries (one unplastered unroofed wicker-work in the foreground) are positioned close to the huts. The presence of tall palms and banana nearby are evidence for good water supply at the foot of this hill. The image seems to have been taken sometime in January 1879 when Buchta travelled through Acholi country en route to Bunyoro.

Women stay in a special birthing hut to have their babies. Deborah, the main informant,  constructed this hut for her daughter. The hut entrance faces north. After the birth a shelter of grasses is put round the hut. If the baby is a girl they stay for 4 days afterwards, 3 days if it is a boy. Traditionally the boy would be wrapped in special bark cloth. Today all babies are wrapped in cotton. (See 2008.78.1.1) Patti Langton [16/11/2010]

A young girl sits on a mat in front of the entrance to her hut, making pottery coils, BIRI BIRI. In front of her is the beginning of a pot, about five coils are already built up on top of an old pottery base, KAGYE,  which is used to create the shape. The girl is kneading, TENGUE,  the clay LUDRI. She keeps it moist with water in a metal pot beside her. There is a sequence of this pot being made, unfortunately I've not quite filed it in the right order, but you can see where it goes wrong by the number of coils! The long stick beside her is her walking stick, she had polio as a young child.  (See 2008.78.2.90-101; also 2008.78.1.12). Patti Langton [30/03/2009]

A friend of informant Deborah, Naomi Tudrinwa, is firing her pots, a continuation of 2008.78.175 and 210 onwards. Images of pottery-making can be seen between 2008.78.2.90-101 and in 2008.78.2.150 Naomi herself is making a pot. Naomi has friends to help her fire the pots. They have prepared the firing materials between three tree trunks, and in this image Naomi is using a long-handled digging stick to push the straw and sticks. The pots can be seen behind her between smouldering logs. They had placed bark and sticks over the ground, put the pots among them and cover the pots with more stick to fire them.  Patti Langton [30/06/2009]

Deborah, main informant, with her daughters and their husbands. She has 4 daughters. Also  pictured is Rachel the young translator. The people sit on a bed made of logs across a log base. Sitting on the steps on Lui school, a young sanza player creates lovely music, watched by a young boy. I recorded some of his music. One of the songs tells of a boy and girl who want to marry, but the mother of the girl doesn't like the boy so he can't marry her. [Patti Langton 09/03/2009]

Close up image of decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.   It has ABINY KHAR... 1939.98 carved at the top. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid them. Informant Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound (See 2008.78.1.38). Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has three 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. Patti Langton [26/05/2009]

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) stuck into the ground with a shorter notched post (lingi) for hunting-magic offerings, usually fowl sacrifice. During drought the rain-post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A set of old stone axe-heads and other stone tools, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home along with his hair clippings in a pot beneath the eaves of his stake-walled hut. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from [light leakage on negative?].

A stone mound erected over a woman's grave (dodo) with two carved posts tallying the number of large or dangerous animals killed by her husband as a means of honouring her. The post on the right has a tin basin affixed to the top, possibly for receiving offerings.

A rain-making shrine of an unusual type compared to other Bongo rain-posts (riyak), and rather more like in form a Zande tuka or ancestral shrine. It was situated under a large tree, with ground swept well around it. The female operator of the shrine threw water over it with an invocation to spirits during drought, since she was widely considered to be possessed and closely associated with ancestral spirits. Directly behind it is a grave mound with forked tally grave post [image cloudy at centre].

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [cloudy image].

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them). Three are visible in this image: the tip of a carved post in the likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then to the right a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly in the foreground a forked post tallying five buffalo, with a ?bowl and ?piece of matting stuck on it.

Her hair is set in the typical Kanuri fashion of a single braid on the forehead and a triangular red clip at the top. She is gazing at a frame held out before her.

Portrait of a Kanuri Chief's wife. She has scarification on her face and hair braided with a single braid hanging over her forehead in typical Kanuri style for a married woman, and a red clip on the top. She has two gold and green earrings in one lobe.
Portrait of a Kanuri man with typical facial scarification. He is wearing a red embroidered cap and indigo robes.
A Kanuri man making shoes. He is stitching together elements of the sole of the shoe.
An advertisement in Maiduguri for 'The New Nigerian Barber, with all styles of hair dressing headdie shampo & stretching', displaying six different hairstyle types.

Kanuri Chief Lawan Mustafa seated outside his in Konduga Village, 25 miles east of Maiduguri. Mustafa is the headman of the village and is wearing an expensive embroidered blue cap and robe. Edward Ross' truck is parked outside Lawan Mustafa's home.
A Kanuri silversmith hammering silver openwork horse ornaments on a small anvil.

A Kanuri man, Ali Kulloma, making a beeswax pestle. The wax will then encased in mud to create a mould, once dried the wax is heated and poured out before the mould is buried in sand and molten brass poured in.

An older woman at a Kanuri market in Maiduguri selling peanuts and sliced okra, which would be added to soups. The woman has facial scarification and her hair is dressed with a single braid hanging in the middle of her forehead with a plastic hair ornament worn at the top. The woman has pink millet stalk ear plugs and dark eye-makeup under her eyes.

A close-up showing the meshwork of mopane poles packed with mud, the preferred Mbukushu method of building in Boseja ward at this time. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River. This hut was in the plot of Jobe Phezo, a woman living in Boseja ward.

Close up view of a lolwapa fence made from the stems of mokodi (wild sage), in the plot of Manyema Dibonke, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward. He came to Main in 1995 from Nxomoxao near Mohembo, and eventually found this plot with his elder brother in 1997, looking for a better life.

A hut under construction. This shows the technique commonly adopted by Mbukushu migrants in Boseja ward at this time, creating a dense wall of moping poles (dipalalo), which will then be strengthened with horizontally bound sticks (dithupa) to create a meshwork, over which mmu wa seolo (anthill soil) will be plastered. If people could find dung to mix with it, they would, but there were no cattle grazing locally.
A plate basket incorporating animals in the design. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.

The homestead of Moffat Mokhawa in Matlapaneng ward, showing his planting of hedging, shrubs and fruit trees around the plot. In the foreground is a Mophane tree pollarded for share, and to the right of the mud-plastered hut is a Pepper tree (Schinus molle).

Two men wearing dammur cloth, photographed by Evans-Pritchard during his brief two day visit to the hill, the peoples of which speak a dialect of Burun. He also noted however that some people identified themselves as an exogenous group known as Fuin, who formed an aristocratic group with a 'king' who was frequently in danger of regicide from other potential leaders. But this group seems mostly to have been absorbed by Burun.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the south face and east side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela F, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This is the most graceful and most elaborately decorated of all the Quirigua stelae. [...] South face: on the pedestal is a large grotesque head or mask, and above it is the upper part of a human figure with hands raised and the palms turned outwards; above this human head is a grotesque mask with the wing of a serpent-bird on either side of it. [...] The graceful arrangement of the feather-work on the upper part of this monument is well worthy of note.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 6) to 9.16.10.0.0, 1 Ahau 3 Zip (Maya calendar), or A.D. 761 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Considered to be one of the great masterpieces of Mesoamerican sculpture, the monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph P, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This great monument, which must weigh nearly twenty tons, stands, like the other monolithic animals, on a foundation of three large flat stones, which are not visible in the photographs. When first found it presented a most enigmatic appearance, for it was not until the earth had been dug away around the base that the great hands or flippers could be seen, which proved the main design to be the representation of a great turtle. The head of the animal, which faces nearly south, is surrounded by a hieroglyphic inscription.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 16) to 9.18.5.0.0, 4 Ahau 13 Ceh (Maya calendar), or A.D. 795 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years as various different animals, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a Cosmic Monster with a mountain on its back. The monument was created during the reign of Sky Xul and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the north face of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela D, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'The north face of the monument is slightly broader than the south face, and is much the same in design. The great grotesque head on the pedestal is furnished with scrolls, which apparently spring from the cheeks and spread over the ears; attached to each of these scrolls is a human head with the face turned upwards.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 4) to 9.16.15.0.0, 7 Ahau 18 Pop (Maya calendar), or A.D. 766 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

Portrait of Kiingi Taawhiao (Tukaroto Matutaera Potatau Te Wherowhero Tawhiao c.1822-1894) with tā moko (face tattoo) and wearing kahu kiwi (kiwi feather cloak) and ear pendant. Tāwhiao was leader of the Waikato tribes, the second Māori King, and a religious figure. He was a member of the Ngati Mahuta hapū of Waikato.
[Image vignetted and details retouched.]

Group of Maori male prisoners seated on the ground with six soldiers (?militia) standing above them. Most of the Maori prisoners are wearing hats and some are wearing cloaks, blankets, or piupiu (a grass skirt). The soldiers are wearing uniforms, some with shoulder sashes, and carrying rifles. The photograph may have been taken during the East Cape War of 1865-1868, an anti-European uprising in the region.
Group of men, women and children (including half-cast boys) in Maori dress outside house of raupo (bulrush) type with wooden and corrugated iron addition.

The body is decorated with a head wreath of leaves and black ribbon, and positioned under sheets and black cloth onto which a greenstone mere (club) is laid.  The body is propped up on woven mats, with korowai (tag cloaks) hanging behind on porch wall.  A woman wearing in European clothing with blanket as over-skirt, sits in attendance. Mbulu ngulu. Reliquary guardian figure of wood, plated with hammered copper and brass. In the centre is a human face with protruding forehead, oval eyes, a pointed triangular nose, and convex brow indicating that he is male. Ngha. A: Drum and B: beater, (Gurung) NGhaanrdaan (C-K). Side frame made of wood of Chaingi tree. The wood can only be cut down on a ' good' day (determined by astrology) - all materials must be obtained on a ' good' day and the drum must be assembled on a single ' good' day. This wood is difficult to get, since it does not grow everywhere and many people do not recognize it. The strip of wood is shaped by putting it in a circular hole in the ground where it is left for fifteen days. Sidelacing made of Kre creeper or vine. Skin made of goat, ideal to have the skin of a goat which has been killed by a tiger or a leopard, but this is not always possible. Old goat skin is much better and stronger. Forked piece of wood across inside of drum used as handle. This type of drum is only made and used by shamans. This one for Pa-chyu shamans and Khhlyeprin makes similar drums but the size is a little bigger. This is an old drum, possibly made by Yarjung's grandfather. Used for some mortuary and healing rituals. ' Good' rhythms for curing rituals, ' Dead', not so good rhythms used for funerals. Only shamans understand what the different rhythms mean. Rhythms must be read. The sound is better when heated, and is usually heated in the fire. This is an old drum and it makes a very strong sound, so there is no need to heat. But new drums must be heated before playing. B) Stick made of strip of bamboo; Good

Thangka. Hanging - Lamaist hanging or ' tanka' . " This is a printed ' tanka' (Tibetan ' thang- ka'), usually kept in a temple. The general style of the ' tanka' is in the Tibetan tradition, but there are several aspects which are characteristically Mongolian, particularly the prayers in Mongol script down the sides and bottom, and the representation of a Mongol felt tent ('ger') centre left. The ' tanka' represents the Green Tara (centre), seated on a lotus and holding in her left hand a long- stemmed lotus flower. She is the consort of Avalokita, now thought to be incarnate in the Dalai Lamas, and she is one of the most popular deities in Tibet and Mongolia, both with Lamas and laity. The green version of Tara is more common than the white version, which according to Waddell, is believed by the Mongols to be incarnate in the White Tsar. This ' tanka' has nine Taras (a much more common number is twenty-one, each of which has a particular quality for helping people. The ' tanka' represent,apart from the Taras: the sun (right) and the moon (left), temples, snakes, camels and riders, etc. Centre top is (probably) the demon Damdin, defender of the faith, or Lha- mo, a demoness defender of the faith. The deity is surrounded by flames, indicating that it is one of the fierce deities, riding a horse, and slaying a ?dragon. Centre bottom is (probably) the female deity Narici, meaning ' the resplendent', a goddess of the dawn. She is linked with the pig, and here she is seated in a chariot drawn by pigs. In her usual form she has three faces and eight hands, but here she seems to have only one face and two hands. She holds various weapons in her hands; in her fiercer forms she is the companion of the warrior-Damdin. Sometimes she is called ' the diamond sow' . Many scenes in this ' tanka' remain unexplained, such as the two figures left bottom kneeling beside one another, or the strangely medieval boats on a lake right centre-bottom. The ' tanka' was obtained from Buryat ASSR, in 1972, but it is not known if it was manufactured there or in Mongolia."

Eleven wooden clothes pegs (.1-.11), each made from a single, roughly cylindrical piece of wood that has been split up the middle. Model of a tent (.1) constructed of sticks inserted into a blue painted wooden board and covered with a loosely woven brown-beige cloth pinned into position with short wooden pins. The tent has a high peak with cloth rolled up to form an entrance, is carpeted with lace-trimmed red cloth, and has a metal brazier nailed in the centre with a pot hanger positioned over the top. Associated with the tent are three pillows (.2-4); one of striped beige and peach ticking, one trimmed with lace and one blue with blue and peach pattern. Four rectangles of cloth (.5-8) are also associated; three of embroidered cotton edged with wide lace, one with printed floral pattern and purple edging.

Tamata. Votive offering. Representation of a baby modelled in yellow wax. The eyes are represented by black-eyed beans pushed into the wax. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension. The wax in the neck area is badly cracked and bits have crumbled away.

Tamata. Votive offering. Elongated and stylised leg modelled in green wax. The foot is represented by a square slab of wax with scratched on lines to show the divisions between the toes. The leg is slightly bent at the knee and a loop of string threaded through a hole above the knee suggests a point of suspension. Broken above knee.

Keyring of protective charms. Large blue glass disc decorated with concentric white, yellow and blue glass rings intended to ward off the evil eye (nazar). bag - Fish skin purse made by Matleena Fofanoff in two halves in the traditional style of Sámi coffee and salt bags. The bottom half is made of three pieces of fish (salmon) skin ‘leather’ - this forms the main body of the bag. The top half (which forms the area which is tied to close) is made from one piece of fish (pike) skin leather - this is sewn together with sinew thread (sinew thread is made from reindeer sinew). The tie is made from a twisted pike skin leather cord - both ends are decorated with a fish vertabrae. The body part of the purse is decorated with a piece of red woollen cloth upon which have been sewn plastic beads in a pattern made up of five diamond shapes. The beads are coloured white, blue and yellow.

A man's paddle that may have been cut down to create a woman's paddle. Carved design on one face of the lanceolate blade with 5 faces and several ' eyes', with plain, toothed curves, zigzags, and bar.. Slightly raised shaft top with two projecting ovals at the sides, that are incised with a knob and bar design, inside a ring border. The whole appears to be encrusted with a thin layer of mud or brown paint.

Representation - Long and narrow curved bar with raised pierced mid-rib and pig's head at either end. Mid-rib piercings are mostly oval in shape with triangular tongues left in their centres. Many red fibre tassels are tied through them. Either side of mid-rib bar are incised lines and nicks and some projecting ovals and curves which have core rings and look like ' eyes' . Painted red inside incisions, occasional black outlines, mainly white background. Under surface painted black, with remains of white and red. Series of holes pierce through from underside on one side of mid-rib only. Pig's heads have prominent tusks and elongated snouts, with rough eye rings or eye cavities and horizontal slit mouths. Painted with red and black lines against white background. Wrapped in brown paper and tied to bar is a long coil of white feathers bound with bast fibre which must have ornamented the board at one stage. Mid-rib broken and part missing, bar mended with glue, fibre tassels fraying, paint worn. Said to be loot from Tshambuli. Original accession notes: " A long carved board with longitudinal ridge. At each end is a carved representation of a pig's head. The Iatmul knew nothing of the uses of this object. In the American Natural History Museum there are comparable objects collected by Dr. Fortune from Tshuosh in the Turu area." Poor

Pukuru putkuli. A woman's body cloth made from two large rectangles of cream cotton cloth that have been folded lengthways and sewn together. One cloth is woven with thick red stripes that have been embroidered with geometric patterns in black, and one thick blue stripe towards one end with stripes of black embroidery running towards the edge; the other cloth is woven with blue and red stripes towards one end.
Pencil drawing - 1 unaccessioned portrait in pencil on paper of a Toda woman in profile. The back of the mount is inscribed 'Toda / Mrs Milward' in pencil.

A necklace consisting of small faceted gold gilt beads strung onto two lengths of plant fibre, attached by a central a row of red glass beads set in circles of spiralled copper alloy wire. There are dangling pointed gold gilt beads along the bottom row. It is fastened by a loop of plant fibre and a gilt bead at the ends.
A necklace consisting of small faceted gold gilt beads, pointed beads with small round projections, and small wooden beads towards the ends; they are strung onto a length of plant fibre.

Pennanular gilded brass armlet. Made from sheet metal, rolled over at the edges to create a hollow tubular shape; protruding pyramidal forms around the outer surface; gilded on the outer surface. One of four armlets, 1944.22.6.13-16.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Rama, an Irula man.
Necklace  - Necklace comprising imitation coins on maroon-coloured thread. Worn by young men and women
Bead necklace. Worn by men and women.

Musical instrument, consisting of a cane with pegs for two strings, conventionalized bird head at one end remote from pegs, eleven separate bridges attached with black gum, and three gourd resonators lashed on below.
Carved bamboo flute with four stops.

Kubadhi. A pair of men's leather sandals. Made from at least four layers of dark brown leather sewn together with white thread. The upper sections are made from light and dark brown leather. The sandals are bound together by a tied strip of plant fibre. Made by men and women.

Dzhibadone. A long sleeved cotton waistcoat or jacket, with a double breasted front with metal hook and eye fastenings. The fabric is blue with cream and red vertical stripes; panels of red and brown fabric have been added to the armpits. There is black trim around the neck, front opening and cuffs, and along the front fastenings. The cuffs are fastened with black glass beads. Inside the jacket is lined with cream cotton.
A hat, possibly a fez, made from cream colour felt, of cylindrical shape, with a short projection on the top.

A hooded coat or cloak made from un-spun grey wool, with long sleeves with open seams along the the underarms, two side pockets, and fastened by black and white cotton toggle buttons along the front. The edges of the coat are trimmed with white cotton cord, and the front opening is trimmed with black and white cotton cord. Some of the interior seams are possibly secured by felting.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, green, maroon, blue, white and pink. Tied together.

Beaded ornament in the form of a snake, comprising a long, white textile tube decorated with coloured glass beads, with a lozenge-shaped head and loops of white and blue beads for the tail. The head is black with white eyes, and has white, blue-green and beige chevrons on the underside. The body has blue, red, black, white, pink, yellow, and beige circles on a green background on one side, and beige on the underside.
Wooden paddle with cylindrical handle and flat, triangular blade.
Spear. Leaf-shaped, socketed iron head with mid-rib and narrow shank. Tapering wooden shaft.
Ngoohit Nyigit.  An armlet worn on upper arm, worn only by warriors. Made from two warthog tusks, joined together by hide wrapped around the ends and stitched together with fibre.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red and opaque white beads.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red and opaque white beads.
Half gourd used by men for drinking milk. The gourd is decorated with geometric grooves in a checkerboard pattern. There is a small perforation at the stem, through which is a fibre loop.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped with a prominent midrib; split socket. The shaft has a circular cross-section, and terminates with a metal ferrule tapering to a point. There is a ring of hide around the ferrule, about halfway down.

Bowl with handles, said to be a royal milk pan. Large circular bowl carved from wood with two small semi-circular handles below the rim; flat base, flaring walls and slightly everted rim; stained dark brown to red.
A pipe, with a burnished black pottery bowl [.1] and a wooden stem [.2]. The bowl is rounded, with a ridge down each side and an upturned point at the front of the rim.

Tapering oval wooden beer cup or food bowl, covered in a red pigment, which rests upon a pedestal foot of four broadly triangular supports and a longitudinally ridged oval base. Threaded through two of the supports is a circular tied strand of plant fibre.
Wooden ladle carved from a single piece of wood. Bowl deep and circular in shape. Handle has a semicircular cross-section and tapers towards the end.

Charm or amulet shaped like a crescent. Made from red cloth or fibre corved with a fine net of knotted string; small white and blue glass beads strung at interval in the net; two lengths of plant fibre cord inserted in crescent.
